subsection: 9. Culture and religion: the Irish language, Vatican II and the communications revolution

notes.h: Starting point: church, language and isolation around 1949
notes.b: To judge how much changed between 1949 and 1989, you need to know what the starting point was: a state built around the Irish language and the Catholic Church, and cut off from much of the outside world.
points: The 1937 Constitution (Article 8) made Irish the national language and first official language, with English recognised as a second official language. State policy was to revive Irish through schools, the civil service and the Gaeltacht, the mainly western and south-western districts where Irish was still spoken daily.
The Catholic Church shaped schools, health and social policy, giving the state a strongly Catholic ethos, and Mass attendance was very high.
The Mother and Child dispute of 1951, in which the bishops opposed Noel Browne's health scheme and the government dropped it, showed the church at the peak of its influence over policy.

Ireland in the 1950s was isolated and suffered heavy emigration, which drained rural areas and the Gaeltacht. From 1958 and through the 1960s, economic expansion, urbanisation and rising living standards opened the country to outside influences, which is why old certainties came under pressure.
notes.tip: Essays on culture and religion reward a clear thread from the old, enforced model of the 1940s and 1950s to flexibility and choice later, so keep this starting point in mind when you argue about change.

notes.h: Changing attitudes to the Irish language, 1949–1973
notes.b: Irish was the first official language of the state, but it was losing ground as a community language, and by the 1960s public attitudes were turning against compulsion.
points: Official policy rested on compulsion. Irish was a compulsory school subject, a pass in Irish was required for the Leaving Certificate (the final secondary school exam) and Irish was needed for entry to the civil service.

Gael Linn, founded in 1953, tried to promote the language positively through popular means, including records, the Amharc Éireann newsreel from 1956 and the feature film Mise Éire in 1959, a documentary on the years before 1916.
The Gaeltacht was in decline in the 1950s because of emigration, so the state set up Gaeltarra Éireann in 1957 to encourage industry in Irish-speaking areas and give people a reason to stay.

The Commission on the Restoration of the Irish Language reported in 1963, and a government White Paper of 1965 accepted the aim of restoration but proposed a more flexible approach, showing that policy was softening.

The Language Freedom Movement, founded in 1966, campaigned against compulsory Irish, arguing that compulsion turned pupils against the language, and it provoked counter-campaigns from defenders of the language.

In 1973 the Fine Gael-Labour government, with Richard Burke as Minister for Education, ended the rule that students must pass Irish to gain the Leaving Certificate. The requirement for civil service entry was also relaxed later.
Do not overstate the 1973 change. Only the compulsory pass at the Leaving Certificate ended, and Irish itself stayed a compulsory school subject.
notes.tip: Examiners want a thread from enforced duty to flexibility and choice in 1973, backed by dated evidence such as Gael Linn 1953, the 1963 Commission, the 1965 White Paper and the LFM 1966. Do not confuse Gael Linn, which promoted Irish, with the LFM, which opposed compulsion.

notes.b: From the late 1960s, Irish speakers themselves pressed for services in their own language, and the state responded by creating new broadcasting and development bodies.
points: The Gaeltacht Civil Rights Movement, formed in 1969, demanded better services and Irish-language radio because the state offered none. In 1970 it ran a pirate station (an unlicensed broadcaster), Saor Raidió Chonamara.

Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting from Connemara on Easter Sunday, 2 April 1972, giving Irish speakers a regular, official service in their own language, so they no longer needed pirate broadcasts. Do not confuse it with the pirate Saor Raidió Chonamara of 1970.
Bord na Gaeilge was set up in 1975 to coordinate efforts to promote Irish.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, created in 1980, took over responsibility for the economic and social development of the Gaeltacht. It later absorbed the work of Gaeltarra Éireann, set up in 1957.

The Irish language retained its symbolic status, but the number of everyday speakers continued to decline outside the Gaeltacht, which itself was shrinking. Compulsion had also left many pupils indifferent.
notes.tip: Name the bodies with their dates and keep them apart: Bord na Gaeilge 1975 coordinates promotion, Údarás na Gaeltachta 1980 develops the Gaeltacht. A list of institutions without a judgement on whether the language actually recovered scores poorly.

notes.b: Ó hEithir was a writer, journalist and broadcaster whose work in Irish and English brought the culture of the Gaeltacht and the Irish language to a modern audience.
points: Breandán Ó hEithir was born in 1930 on Inis Mór, one of the Aran Islands, and died in 1990.
He was a journalist and a broadcaster with RTÉ, reporting on current affairs, culture and sport in Irish and English, and he wrote for newspapers, including a regular column.
His novel Lig Sinn i gCathú (1976), a satirical novel about the life of a Galway student, was widely read in Irish, and he translated it himself as Lead Us into Temptation in 1978.
His Over the Bar (1984) was a personal account of the GAA, and The Begrudger's Guide to Irish Politics (1986) was a witty account of political life, written in English.

He was a participant in the cultural change of the period rather than a leader of a movement. He presented Irish as a living medium for modern subjects, not as a duty, which fitted the move away from compulsion.
Contemporaries valued him as a bridge between the Gaeltacht and the English-speaking world and as a rare Irish-language writer with a wide readership.
Later critics regard him as one of the most accomplished bilingual writers and broadcasters of his generation.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on Ó hEithir, give his birthplace and year, his work as journalist and broadcaster with RTÉ, his writing in Irish and English, three named books with dates, and his significance. Each correct, dated statement earns marks.

notes.b: Alongside the debate about the language, traditional music enjoyed a revival that made Irish culture feel modern and attractive rather than a duty.
points: Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann was founded in Mullingar in 1951, and the fleadh cheoil (music festival and competition) held from 1952 helped to spread traditional music and dance.

Seán Ó Riada composed the score for Mise Éire (1959). From 1961 his group Ceoltóirí Chualann played traditional music in a concert style, which brought it to a wider audience. Do not confuse the group with Comhaltas.

Ó Riada's Ceol an Aifrinn (1968), the Mass in Irish set to sean-nós-style music (the old unaccompanied singing style) for the church at Cúil Aodha, linked the music revival to the changes brought by Vatican II.
The Chieftains were formed in 1962, and the Clancy Brothers, The Dubliners and later Planxty made Irish ballads and traditional music popular at home and abroad.
The revival gave Irish culture a modern commercial and international dimension, and it reduced the old divide between a rural traditional culture and urban popular culture.

notes.h: Vatican II and the Irish church
notes.b: The Second Vatican Council, the worldwide meeting of Catholic bishops in Rome, changed Catholic worship and the church's relationship with other Christians and the modern world.
points: Pope John XXIII opened the council on 11 October 1962 and it closed on 8 December 1965 under Paul VI. Irish bishops, including McQuaid, attended.
The council allowed the Mass to be said in the vernacular (the everyday language) instead of Latin, so people could follow it. The first Masses in English in Ireland were celebrated in 1965.
Priests now faced the congregation, laypeople could be readers and distribute communion, and parish councils and lay organisations were encouraged, giving ordinary Catholics a bigger role.

The council promoted ecumenism, closer relations and dialogue between Christian churches. The Catholic ban on Catholics attending Trinity College Dublin was lifted in 1970, and the first formal inter-church talks with the main Protestant churches in Ireland were held at Ballymascanlon, Co. Louth, in 1973.
It declared in 1965 that religious freedom was a right, which weakened the claim that the Catholic Church should have a special position in law.
Many Irish Catholics welcomed the changes, but others, mostly older, felt unsettled by the loss of Latin and old devotions, because these had been part of their lifelong habits of worship.
Vatican II also encouraged people to think for themselves on moral questions and to follow their conscience, which contributed to a questioning of church authority.
notes.tip: Know what Vatican II changed (vernacular Mass, lay roles, ecumenism, conscience and religious freedom) and how Irish Catholics reacted. At Ordinary Level give the opening and closing dates, the Pope, the first English Masses in 1965 and priests facing the people.

notes.h: Key personality: Archbishop John Charles McQuaid (part 2: Vatican II and overall evaluation)
notes.b: McQuaid, Archbishop of Dublin from 1940 to 1972, was the most powerful churchman in Ireland, and he was cautious about the changes brought by the council. His reaction shows the gap between the council's openness and his conservative style.
points: McQuaid was born in 1895 in Cootehill, Co. Cavan. He was a participant in church-state relations, with direct access to ministers, and his influence had peaked in the Mother and Child dispute of 1951, when the bishops opposed a state health scheme.
He attended Vatican II and on returning reassured Dubliners that the council would not disturb their faith, a message of reassurance in tune with his conservative outlook.
He implemented liturgical reforms in Dublin, but slowly. He was wary of ecumenism, which he regarded as risky for Catholic doctrine, and of lay initiatives outside the control of the clergy.
His reach showed in the McGahern case: John McGahern's novel The Dark was banned in 1965, and McGahern lost his teaching post at a Dublin primary school after pressure involving the Archbishop.

He was also involved in education, social work and the building of new churches and schools in the Dublin suburbs, and the Catholic Social Service Conference, set up in 1941, was one of his charitable bodies.
He retired in January 1972, at the end of more than thirty years as archbishop, and died in 1973. He was succeeded by Dermot Ryan.
Contemporaries admired his efficiency and devotion to the church, but critics complained of his authoritarian style and his readiness to intervene in politics and in people's lives.
Historians, notably John Cooney in his biography John Charles McQuaid: Ruler of Catholic Ireland (1999), portray him as a ruler whose style came to seem out of date.
Other historians stress his building of schools and welfare services. They argue that the decline of church power came from social change as much as from his policies, so he cannot be blamed alone.
notes.tip: For McQuaid and Vatican II, state his reaction (reassurance, slow reform, wariness of ecumenism), contrast his authority with the council's openness, and give a verdict using both contemporary and historian views. The Mother and Child material adds context but cannot be the whole answer.

notes.b: Secularisation is the decline of religion's influence over public life, institutions and personal behaviour. The evidence for it in Ireland points both ways, which is why historians treat the period as a slow shift rather than a sudden break.
points: A survey in 1973 and 1974 found about nine in ten Catholics attending Mass weekly, so practice remained high even as other signs of change appeared.

Pope Paul VI's encyclical (a formal papal letter) Humanae Vitae in 1968 reaffirmed the ban on artificial contraception, and many Irish married Catholics found it difficult to accept. It was a papal decision after the council, not a Vatican II reform.

Vocations to the priesthood and religious life began to fall from the late 1960s, and fewer young people entered seminaries and convents, which shows that commitment was weakening even while Mass attendance stayed high.
Pope John Paul II visited Ireland from 29 September to 1 October 1979, and a Mass in the Phoenix Park drew over a million people, but the visit did not halt the long-term shift.
Secularisation advanced through the 1970s and 1980s, helped by education, television, emigration and contact with Europe, which exposed people to other ways of life.
Pluralism, acceptance that a society contains different beliefs and traditions, none privileged by the state, was at the centre of the 1983 referendum on abortion and the 1986 referendum on divorce.

The results showed that traditional views remained strong: the Eighth Amendment on abortion was carried in September 1983 by about two-thirds, and the divorce proposal was rejected in June 1986 by about two-thirds.
notes.tip: Link Vatican II to secularisation with evidence both ways: high Mass attendance, the 1979 visit and the 1983 and 1986 votes on one side, falling vocations and Humanae Vitae on the other. Define each concept in one sentence, then illustrate it, and do not confuse secularisation, pluralism and ecumenism.

notes.b: Censorship is the official banning or restriction of books, films and other material judged indecent, obscene or otherwise unacceptable. The system built in the 1920s and 1940s was relaxed in the 1960s as attitudes changed.
points: The Censorship of Publications Act 1929 set up a board that could ban books for being indecent or obscene, and the Act of 1946 added an appeals board. Thousands of books were banned, including works by leading Irish writers.
John McGahern's novel The Dark was banned in 1965, and he lost his teaching post after pressure involving the Archbishop of Dublin. The case became a symbol of the censorship of the time.
The Censorship of Publications Act 1967, introduced by the Minister for Justice, Brian Lenihan, provided that a ban lasts twelve years unless renewed, so many thousands of titles were released.
Film censorship became more liberal during the 1960s and 1970s, as television and cinema showed material from abroad.
Contraceptives and publications about them were covered by separate laws until the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, so the 1967 relaxation did not change that area.
Broadcasting was controlled in a different way, through the powers of the minister over RTÉ, rather than by the publications board.
notes.tip: Keep the Acts apart: 1929 and 1946 created and adapted the censorship system, while 1967 relaxed it. A short answer on the 1967 Act should state the twelve-year limit and the many titles freed.

notes.b: From the 1960s, better transport, telephones, newspapers, radio, television and computers ended the isolation of the 1950s.
points: Car ownership rose sharply between 1960 and 1980, and better roads, bus services and air travel reduced rural isolation by making it easier to travel and to meet outsiders.
Telephone services, once poor and slow to expand, were improved, and in 1984 Bord Telecom Éireann was set up to run them as a separate state company.
Television reached most households in the 1960s and early 1970s, and RTÉ 2 started in 1978, bringing more programmes and choice. British channels could be received in much of the east and north.
The Irish Times under the editor Douglas Gageby, from 1963, became a forum for new ideas, and magazines such as Magill, founded in 1977, expanded political journalism.
Pirate radio stations grew in the 1970s and 1980s, challenging RTÉ's monopoly (its sole right to broadcast), and the Radio and Television Act 1988 licensed independent local radio.
Computers were adopted in business and government from the 1970s, and American firms such as Digital opened plants in Ireland, laying the base for the electronics industry.
These changes exposed people to a wider range of ideas and lifestyles, and helped to break down the isolation on which traditional authority had rested.
notes.tip: Argue that the revolution ended isolation and weakened traditional authority, naming separate media (transport, telephones, newspapers, radio, television, computers), each with a date or example and an effect on attitudes. Better answers also note limits, such as British media, slow telephone growth and the church's continued influence.

notes.b: Judging this period means weighing real change against its limits, and comparing how people at the time saw it with how historians see it now.
points: Achievements: the Irish language gained broadcasting and institutions, traditional music was revived and reached a world audience, the church accepted liturgical reform and ecumenism, and censorship was relaxed.
Limits: the language continued to decline as a community language, the compulsion debates left many pupils indifferent, and the church's leadership, especially under McQuaid, was slow to adapt.
Contemporary view: traditionalists feared that television and liberal reform threatened Irish identity and Catholic values, while reformers regarded the changes as overdue.
Later view: historians regard the period as the start of the shift to a more secular and pluralist society, with the church retaining strong influence on law and public life well into the 1980s.
notes.tip: Reward in essays goes to a judgement, not a list. Say whether the language actually recovered, and weigh evidence both ways for secularisation, such as high Mass attendance against falling vocations.

keyTerms.definition: The movement for closer relations and dialogue between Christian churches, promoted by Vatican II.
The decline in the influence of religion over public life, institutions and personal behaviour.
The official banning or restriction of books, films and other material considered indecent, obscene or otherwise unacceptable.
The acceptance that a society contains different beliefs and traditions, none of which should be privileged by the state.
The Second Vatican Council of 1962 to 1965, which reformed Catholic worship and the church's relations with other faiths and the modern world.
A Mass said in the language of the people instead of Latin, introduced in Ireland from 1965.
The group founded in 1966 that campaigned against compulsory Irish in schools and public service.
The organisation founded in 1953 to promote the Irish language through popular means such as films, records and newsreels.
The districts, mainly in the west and south-west, where Irish remained the community language.
The organisation founded in 1951 to promote traditional Irish music, song and dance.
The 1968 papal encyclical that reaffirmed the Catholic ban on artificial contraception.
